title: Judge Loop and Modular Tests
eyebrow: house-rules · fix proposal · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: judge blocking fix and modular tests

short.lead: The end-of-reply judge blocked 12 times in a row even when three different ways had been tried, because its criteria are one sentence and the model is never told what passes. I propose keeping the judge and tuning it: write the criteria down, make them visible to the model, cap the blocks, and name the exact fix in every block. A second part, tests that are independent modules finishing within a minute, extends the design you already approved.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it changes. The choices at the end are yours.

changes: new
What exists today
Three checks run on every Stop, and they do not know about each other.

The judge is the Stop entry of type prompt in hooks.json. Its criteria are one sentence: flag a claim that something cannot be done, verified, tested or reached unless the reply lists three different methods. It never defines a different method, it sees only the last reply and not the tool calls, and it names no criterion when it blocks. So a model that really ran three checks can still fail, as happened to me four times in this session: the judge said that three ways of reading the same output were one method, and it flagged plain notes of what was not checked. It also keeps no count. The scripted record check (scripts/house_rules/core.py, roadblock_check) already defines methods by class and caps at two blocks; the goal check caps at six on a separate counter. I did not find the transcript of your 12-block session, so the 12 is not reproduced.
A judge with a one-sentence rule and no count.
The same judge with four written criteria and a shared cap.
A model that did the work passes, and a model that did not is told exactly what is missing.
adapt
Write the judge's criteria down
Four numbered criteria, the same text in the judge, the block message and the rules.

The criteria live once, in rules/detail/roadblocks.md. C1, what triggers it: a claim that something is missing, unreachable or impossible and that stops the task. A note of what was not checked is not a trigger when it has the Unverified form. C2, what passes: three attempts in this turn, each aimed at the claimed thing, each from a different method class (existence check, disk search, package database, run it, ask the environment, other source such as CI, git history or docs); reading one output three ways is one method. C3, proof: the attempts appear in the real tool calls, which the judge is shown. C4, the exits: No other method with its reason, NEEDS YOU for a licence, login, purchase or destructive step, or an Unverified line. The judge returns the criterion it failed and the exact thing to add.
One sentence, and the model has to guess what passes.
Four criteria, one source, quoted in every block.
The model always knows what to fix.
adapt
One shared cap
The judge, the record check and the goal check share one counter of two blocks per user message.

After two blocks the reply goes out with a visible warning. The counter resets only when the turn made at least one real tool call after the last block, so a model that keeps working is checked again, while a model that only rewords its reply is not blocked a third time. A prompt hook cannot keep a count, so the choice below decides where the judge runs.
Two counters with caps 2 and 6.
One counter with cap 2.
The worst case is two blocks, not twelve.
adapt
Fewer false alarms
Stop treating ordinary words as roadblocks.

The words "next step" are removed from the stall list, because the house rules themselves tell every reply to end with one next step. The claim list drops the bare phrases "could not", "unable to" and "I can't", and keeps phrases about a missing tool, machine or access. The judge no longer flags a plain Unverified note, which the evidence rule requires. A reply with a NEEDS YOU line is exempt from the goal check too.
_STALL_RE and _ROADBLOCK_RE in core.py.
Narrower lists, and NEEDS YOU exempts both checks.
Normal status replies pass.
new
The passing reply, spelled out
The block message includes the exact lines to paste.

Each block quotes the claim it matched, names the failed criterion (C1 to C4), says which method classes the record already holds and which are missing with a concrete command for each, says how many blocks remain, and shows one of five accepted forms: a Roadblock record of three numbered methods with what each returned, a No other method line with the reason, a NEEDS YOU line, an Unverified line (what, why, and the command that would check it), or a Goal status line. The record is still checked against the real failed tool calls, so invented methods do not pass. The same forms are written into rules/detail/roadblocks.md so the model knows them before it is blocked.
Messages say only to try three methods.
Messages carry a copyable accepted reply.
The model can always find the way out.
new
Tests: the approved design already exists
Another session on your other account designed modular tests, and you approved it on 2026-11-23.

The design is docs/4-systems/modular-tests.md, tracked as issue 575 with children 576 to 582 (rule text, a switch that turns the refactor on and off, a write-time gate that refuses non-modular tests, a skill and audit, converting tools/verify_tools.py, one issue per offshoot suite, and docs). It is not built yet. I will extend it, not redo it. It already gives every module a name and a run-alone command, a --parts runner that chains the modules together, and a conversion skill that proves the old and new runs report the same checks. I ran the whole of verify.py on this branch and measured every part: core 68.9 seconds, safe_git 127.6, design_loop 201.1, writing 8.5, delegation 142.9, docs 46.7 and make_page 105.5. Five of the seven parts are over the 60-second target, and the slowest is over three minutes. That run also had failures: one check in core (the injected rules are 9721 characters and the limit is 9700), three in safe_git, three in delegation, one in make_page, and design_loop stopped without a result line. This branch changes four documentation files and no plugin code, and the same checks pass on main's continuous-integration run (1 minute 22 seconds, on Linux). So the failures come from running on this Windows machine, not from this work; the failing checks involve git -C, file deletion under /tmp, the waitfor timer and node. Fixing them is a separate item.
Design approved, nothing built, issues 575 to 582 open.
Three additions to that design, below.
No duplicate design; one set of issues.
new
Addition 1: a 60-second budget
Any module or run that needs over a minute is flagged and must be split.

Your design does not set a time limit yet. This adds three things: one line in each module's header, a measured time recorded after each run, and a flag that lists every module over 60 seconds with its name and time. The 60-second limit is read from rules/waits.json, so it changes in one place. A step that truly cannot be split, such as one engine build, passes if its reply has one line that starts "Cannot split:" and gives the reason. That line counts against the shared cap of two blocks from the judge fix, so it cannot loop. It lands in the gate (issue 578) and the audit (issue 579).
A 60-second limit on foreground waits exists; no module time is recorded.
A measured flag with a named way out.
A slow module is found and split before it blocks a session.
adapt
Addition 2: each module prints its own result, as it finishes
Results appear per module, in the order they finish.

The approved header names a module and its run-alone command, but does not require each module to print its own PASS or FAIL line and a final RESULT line. This adds that requirement to the gate. It also changes verify.py, which today prints each part only when its turn in the fixed order comes, so a finished part waits behind a slower one. The change prints each part the moment it finishes.
verify.py holds finished output until earlier parts end.
Each module prints when done.
You and the model see results sooner.
new
Addition 3: proof that modules are independent
The conversion skill runs each module alone, then all in shuffled order.

Your design proves that old and new runs report the same checks. That does not prove independence, because a fixed order can hide a module that needs another one's leftovers. This adds a second proof to /house-rules:modular-tests convert: run each module alone, then all modules in a shuffled order, and compare. A mismatch is reported as a hidden dependency between modules and is not fixed automatically.
The proof compares counts only.
Counts, plus runs of each module alone and all modules shuffled.
A hidden dependency is caught during conversion.
risk
Flaws I found in this design
Four known gaps, each with its answer.

One: a stricter, written judge could still disagree with the scripted record check; both read the same criteria text and the same method classes, so they cannot differ on what counts. Two: a model could write fake methods, so the record is checked against real failed tool calls. Three: a shared cap of two with no reset would leave a long unattended run unchecked, so the cap resets after real tool work. Four: I have not confirmed whether Claude Code's own limit of 8 consecutive blocks applies to prompt hooks. Beyond the missing cap, the 12 is unexplained, so the build plan adds a replay of a real session to check.
None of these gaps is handled today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
risk
Flaws I found in the test design
Four known gaps, each with its answer.

One: speed differs by machine, so the time is measured on the machine that runs the tests and recorded, not assumed. Two: a split can hide a real dependency; the shuffled run is the proof, and a failure is reported, not fixed silently. Three: one engine build may never fit in 60 seconds; the Cannot split line is the exit. Four: the 12-block loop came from a judge, so every new refusal in the test design needs the shared cap of two blocks and a copyable accepted reply. Without them it would repeat the same fault.
Nothing guards against these today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
choices: first
Where should the judge run so it can see the attempts and keep a count?
A
Move it into the scripted Stop hook (a nested Haiku call, like the goal check)
It can read the real tool calls, share the counter, and return the failed criterion. It adds up to 22 seconds only when a claim is flagged.
B
Leave it as the prompt hook; add the written criteria and pass on the retry
Smallest change, but it still cannot see the tool calls or count, so it can still misjudge a model that did the work.
The judge has to see the real attempts to be fair, and only a script can see them and keep a count.
share
What should the shared cap be?
A
Two blocks, reset after real tool work
Matches today's record check. The blocks are limited, but long unattended runs are still checked.
B
Two blocks per user message, no reset
Simplest, but an unattended run is no longer checked after two blocks.
C
Three blocks
One more block per reply, so the loop could run one step longer.
A cap of two with a reset ends the loop and still checks long unattended runs.
flask
Where should the 60-second flag live?
A
Inside the approved gate and audit (issues 578 and 579)
One place that refuses, one way out of it, and no second checker to keep in step with the first.
B
A separate checker, tests_budget.py
Easier to test on its own, but it adds a second place that blocks.
The approved design already has the gate and the audit, so the flag belongs in them.

wrapup.summary: A proposal with two linked parts: stop the end-of-reply judge looping, and force tests into independent modules that finish within a minute.
wrapup.changing: Nothing is built. It would edit hooks.json, scripts/house_rules/core.py, rules/detail/roadblocks.md and verify.py, and extend the approved modular-tests design (issues 575 to 582) with a time budget, per-module results and an independence proof.
wrapup.blocking: Your approval and your three choices: where the judge runs, the shared cap, and where the 60-second flag lives.
wrapup.next: After you approve, I record the decision, create one parent issue with a child issue per part, write a build plan, and start with the judge criteria and a replay of 12 blocked replies as a verify.py case.
